title: 3 Ways Hospitals Build Physician and APP Schedules
description: How hospitals and academic medical centers get physician and APP schedules built: a managed service, a spreadsheet, or an enterprise platform like QGenda.
content:
Summary

  • Hospital physician scheduling means coordinating across departments, 24/7 call and credentialing, which is more than general workforce software is usually set up for.
  • The best tool depends on your specific needs: large systems may need an enterprise platform like QGenda, while a smaller department may do fine with a spreadsheet and someone to keep it.
  • Academic medical centers face a unique problem of knowledge loss each year when the chief resident, who manages scheduling, rotates out.
  • For GME programs, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard keeps the program's scheduling knowledge written down and delivers finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements the program tells us apply, with no software for the chief to learn.

If you've ever tried to coordinate a 24/7 call schedule across multiple departments while simultaneously managing credentialing rules, resident rotations, and float pool availability, you already know that hospital scheduling software is a different problem entirely from what most generic reviews describe.

As one health IT professional put it on Reddit: "Nothing is technically broken, but the handoffs are where things fall apart." Another summed it up bluntly: "I haven't seen a single off-the-shelf platform that truly covers ATS + credentialing + scheduling + communications in a clean way."

Hospital scheduling is a multi-system, high-stakes coordination problem, and the tools you choose need to reflect that.

This article looks at three ways hospitals get these schedules built, against the criteria that actually matter in complex hospital environments:

  • Multi-department coordination across the ED, OR, ICU, and specialty floors
  • 24/7 on-call scheduling that balances coverage with staff well-being
  • Credentialing rules that match licensed staff to qualified roles
  • The annual leadership rotation problem unique to academic medical centers, where scheduling knowledge walks out the door when the chief resident changes

Each tool comes with a Best For callout so you can quickly identify which solution fits your specific environment, without wading through a feature checklist that was written for a retail workforce.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

One thing this list does not cover: nursing and hourly staff rostering is a different job with different tools, and we do not build those schedules. If that is what you need, a general workforce platform is a better place to start than anything here. This list is about physician and advanced practice provider schedules.

1. Scheduling Wizard, Best For: Academic Medical Centers and Residency Programs

Best For: GME programs, chief residents, program directors, and fellowship coordinators who need Block, Call, and Clinic schedules built to the ACGME requirements, without the software learning curve.

Scheduling Wizard is the one option here that isn't software.

It's a YC-backed (W26) managed scheduling service: there is nothing to log into; your program sends its rules (ACGME duty hour rules, resident vacation requests, clinic requirements, block rotation preferences) and receives finished schedules delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. There's no implementation project, training sessions, or software to learn.

Why this matters for academic medical centers: In GME scheduling, the problem that repeats every year is knowledge loss. Every July, a new chief resident inherits a scheduling system they've never operated, for a program with dozens of interdependent rules they don't fully understand yet. That usually means weeks of rework, ACGME risk and frustrated residents. With us, the program's rules are written down and kept by our team, not in the outgoing chief's head.

How it handles hospital complexity:

  • The ACGME requirements you tell us apply are built in, not just checked afterwards
  • Block, clinic and call built together, because a resident's block dictates the other two
  • Fair call distribution spreads call burden equitably across the cohort
  • Redrafts for bigger changes, a leave or a rotation move, without the chief rebuilding the schedule by hand

The platform is entirely up to you: keep the one you already use and upload our schedules into it, use the live view we build, or both. Either way, staff keep seeing their day-to-day assignments the way they do now.

For residency programs tired of reinventing the scheduling wheel every July, this managed service approach is a different answer to the question, and for many programs, it's the right one.

What you get: the finished schedule as an Excel or Google Sheets file, and a custom live view if the department wants one. Major redrafts are part of the engagement, which matters on a 24/7 rota, where big changes keep coming through the year. For the specifics, see our page on physician scheduling software.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Best For: Departments with coverage rules that no platform will model cleanly, and someone with the hours to apply them.

Ranked second because it is what many departments actually use, sometimes alongside an enterprise platform they already pay for. A spreadsheet will hold any shift pattern, any site split and any individual arrangement, because a person is doing the reasoning rather than a configuration screen.

It gives out on scale and on arithmetic. Across a 24/7 rota with rotating staff, the dependencies between one schedule and the next are the actual work, and nothing in the file tracks them. Everything the platform below takes on is somebody's evening here.

3. QGenda, Best For: Large Health Systems Needing a Centralized Platform

Best For: Enterprise health systems and large academic centers with dedicated IT and administrative resources to manage a complete, self-service scheduling platform.

QGenda is built as an enterprise-wide physician scheduling platform. It's designed to serve as a single source of truth for provider schedules across an entire health system, from primary care to subspecialty to hospital medicine.

How it handles hospital complexity:

  • Centralized scheduling gives administrators visibility across departments and facilities, reducing the siloing that causes handoff failures
  • Analytics and forecasting help anticipate staffing gaps before they become coverage crises
  • Credentialing integration ties provider qualifications directly into the scheduling logic, so assignments can be checked against each provider's qualifications

Like most enterprise platforms, it comes with a real implementation project, and reviewers often mention the time the initial configuration takes. It's a significant organizational investment, one that pays off at scale, but may be oversized for a single department or smaller program.

Important nuance for GME programs: While QGenda is widely used for schedule viewing and day-to-day provider access, building a complex residency schedule in any platform, with all its ACGME rules and interdependencies, still needs someone on your side to set up the rules and review the result. That is why some programs publish through QGenda and hand the build to a service like Scheduling Wizard.

Decision Matrix: Which Hospital Scheduling Software Fits Your Environment?

Use this as a quick reference to match your hospital's size and complexity profile to the right tool, or combination of tools.

Environment Primary Challenge Recommended Tool(s)
Academic Medical Center / GME Program ACGME compliance, chief resident rotation, block + call + clinic coordination Scheduling Wizard (build) + QGenda, Amion or our live view (viewing)
Large Health System (Enterprise-Wide) Centralized provider scheduling, analytics, credentialing at scale QGenda Physician or APP group with complex coverage Fairness, contracts, site splits Scheduling Wizard (build) + your existing platform Single department with a repeating rota Simple coverage, a few people Excel / Google Sheets with one clear owner

One important takeaway from this matrix: many hospitals will need more than one tool. A large academic medical center might use Scheduling Wizard to build its GME schedules and QGenda as the platform everyone reads them on, at the same time. Focus on closing the gaps in your current stack instead of chasing a single platform that does everything.

Choosing Between a Service, a Spreadsheet and a Platform

Generic software review articles will tell you to compare pricing tiers, mobile app ratings, and integration ecosystems. Those things matter, but they're downstream of a more fundamental question: does this tool actually solve the specific problems that make hospital scheduling hard?

For large health systems managing thousands of providers, QGenda's centralized infrastructure is hard to beat, and plenty of academic centers run it for exactly that reason. For a single department with a repeating rota, a spreadsheet and someone who keeps it current is enough.

But for academic medical centers and GME programs (where the schedule is complex, the stakes are high, and a lot depends on whoever is chief resident this year) the right answer may not be software at all.

Scheduling Wizard is the managed service on this list, so it doesn't ask your chief resident to become a scheduling software expert on top of everything else they're responsible for. Instead, it hands back finished schedules, built to the requirements that apply: the ACGME requirements where the department trains residents, and the department's own coverage, call equity and contractual obligations either way. The institutional knowledge that keeps the schedule running stays put when the chief rotation turns over.

If your residency program is still rebuilding the scheduling system from scratch each year, that's a solvable problem. It just might require a different kind of solution than another software subscription.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does Scheduling Wizard handle the ACGME rules for my program?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They go into the schedule while it is built rather than being flagged afterwards. We do not assume we know your requirements better than you do; we ask.

Do we have to stop using Amion or QGenda to use Scheduling Wizard?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep Amion or QGenda for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

What is the difference between a managed scheduling service and scheduling software?

A managed scheduling service creates the schedule for you, while scheduling software is a tool you use to build the schedule yourself. With a service like Scheduling Wizard, you provide your rules and requests, and our team builds and delivers a finished schedule. Software platforms like QGenda require your team to learn the system, input all the rules, and manage the schedule-building process internally.

How do we handle mid-year changes like a leave or a coverage gap?

For changes that reshape the block, a leave, a resident out for weeks, a change in coverage, you tell us what changed and we rebuild the rest of the schedule to the same rules, with as little disruption to everyone else as the rules allow. Redrafts through the year are part of the service.

What happens to our scheduling process when the chief resident changes every year?

Using Scheduling Wizard solves the problem of knowledge loss from chief resident turnover. Instead of your scheduling expertise walking out the door every July, the institutional knowledge of your program's complex rules, preferences and requests is maintained by our team. The new chief resident doesn't have to learn a complex software or rebuild the system from scratch; they simply submit their cohort's requests to a process that already works.
